Streptocephalus vitreus is a freshwater branchiopod crustacean commonly encountered in ephemeral pools of southern Africa, a habitat that demands rapid development and early reproduction. At a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the incubation period from oviposition to hatching is characteristically brief, with the nauplius larva emerging approximately 30 hours after the brooding adult releases the fertilised eggs. This rapid developmental onset, quantified as 30 hours [ab = 30 hours], corresponds to a crucial stage when the newly hatched free-swimming larva, still reliant on endogenous yolk reserves, begins its progression towards first exogenous feeding at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The dry weight at birth is remarkably low, estimated at 0.000001 grams , a value consistent with the minute egg diameter of 0.23 millimetres and reflecting the extremely small initial body size characteristic of anostracan neonates. This near-microscopic mass, approximately one-millionth of a gram, underscores the extraordinary growth trajectory the species must undergo over its compressed life cycle to achieve a functional adult body size many orders of magnitude larger.

Following the period of rapid somatic growth, which encompasses the nauplius, metanauplius, and juvenile stages, individuals of Streptocephalus vitreus attain the critical developmental milestone of sexual maturation. Under the same laboratory thermal regime maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been determined to be 14 days [tp = 14 days]. The onset of gonadal activity and the formation of a functional reproductive system are accompanied by a significant accumulation of biomass; the dry weight at puberty has been measured at 0.00044 grams . This representative mass, over four hundred times the birth weight, reflects the considerable investment in somatic tissue necessary before the diversion of resources towards gamete production can commence, a pattern typical of branchiopod crustaceans inhabiting temporary waters. It is important to note that this species exhibits determinate growth, ceasing further increases in body size shortly after reaching maturity, a life-history trait that concentrates energetic effort into a brief but intense reproductive window.

The reproductive output of the fairy shrimp is tightly linked to environmental conditions, particularly temperature, which governs both metabolic rate and the timing of key life-history events. At 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females produce clutches containing 42 eggs per brood [N_R_i = 42 eggs per brood], with a typical spawning frequency of 4 broods over an interval of 14 days [F_R_i = 4 broods over an interval of 14 days]. This high fecundity, characteristic of an r-selected life history strategy adapted to ephemeral habitats, ensures population persistence despite the considerable mortality risks associated with unpredictable pond desiccation. The ovigerous female displays a distinctive morphology, carrying the developing brood eggs within a prominent dorsal brood pouch until the fully formed nauplii are ready to be released into the water column. This pattern of repeated reproductive events within a relatively compressed timeframe maximises the total number of offspring that a single berried female can contribute to the next generation before the habitat eventually dries out, with the rapid succession of broods allowing population numbers to build quickly during favourable conditions.

As individuals approach the terminus of their life cycle, the progressive deterioration of physiological function becomes evident, marking the onset of senescence in this short-lived crustacean. The lifespan of Streptocephalus vitreus under controlled conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] has been documented at 30 days [am = 30 days], a relatively short duration consistent with the species鈥 rapid life history pace and typical of many anostracans occupying temporary aquatic habitats. This age-related mortality event occurs after a period of sustained reproductive activity, with the post-reproductive adult exhibiting reduced swimming performance and diminished feeding efficiency. The ultimate dry weight achieved by a fully grown adult prior to the onset of senescence is 0.0013 grams , a value that serves as an upper bound for the species鈥 body mass and represents the culmination of the rapid growth phase. This final mass, attained only after the cessation of moulting and the completion of all somatic growth, is approximately 1300 times greater than the initial dry weight at birth, highlighting the remarkable efficiency with which these crustaceans convert the algal and bacterial resources of their temporary aquatic environment into body tissue over a compressed developmental period.

Comparative analysis of body size metrics across related anostracan species reveals the relatively modest stature of this particular fairy shrimp within the context of the family Streptocephalidae. When considering the dry weight at birth of 1 microgram , it is evident that the neonate is amongst the smallest of the freshwater branchiopods, a trait that likely influences its specific filtration capabilities and vulnerability to predation by aquatic insects and other invertebrate predators common in ephemeral pools. The massive proportional increase to an ultimate dry weight of 1.3 milligrams  is nonetheless comparable to that observed in other genera that occupy similarly unstable, fishless temporary waters, suggesting convergent life-history solutions to the challenges of unpredictable hydroperiods. The entire life cycle, from the activation of the resting egg to the natural death of the post-reproductive adult, is compressed into a narrow seasonal window of opportunity spanning no more than a few weeks. This opportunistic life history culminates in the production of dormant resting eggs, which are the only stage capable of surviving the prolonged dry season that defines the species' challenging habitat, ensuring population persistence across years.
